title: Act I, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: The Ghost says he is Hamlet's father, doomed to walk at night, and that Claudius murdered him by pouring poison into his ear as he slept in his orchard, then seduced Gertrude. He commands revenge but tells Hamlet to leave Gertrude to heaven. Hamlet swears to remember, makes his friends swear secrecy, and warns he may put on an antic disposition.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene V,” how does Shakespeare show the Ghost's revelation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene V, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the Ghost's revelation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene V develops the idea of the Ghost's revelation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene V (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the Ghost's revelation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene V suggests about the Ghost's revelation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act I, Scene V to complicate the reader's understanding of the Ghost's revelation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene V within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the Ghost's revelation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene V alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the Ghost's revelation follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene V and its treatment of the Ghost's revelation. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene V as evidence for a larger claim about the Ghost's revelation in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene V as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the Ghost's revelation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Hamlet accepts the duty of revenge but feels burdened by it. Useful evidence: “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder” (Act I, Scene V, Ghost (speech 12)): The Ghost's command. On characterization: The Ghost reveals the murder: poison poured in the ear. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
